question: What is a webhook?
answer_hinglish:
Webhook ek HTTP callback hai: jab humare system mein koi event hota hai (order paid, user created), hum customer ke registered URL par ek HTTP POST bhej dete hain jisme event ka data hota hai. Customer ko baar baar puchhna nahi padta, hum khud batate hain.

Simple words mein: API mein client server ko call karta hai; webhook mein server client ko call karta hai -- "reverse API". Customer pehle ek endpoint register karta hai ("mujhe order.paid events is URL pe bhejo"), aur phir har matching event pe hum signed POST bhejte hain.

Lekin interview mein main yeh zaroor bolta hoon ki webhook bhejna ek line ka `requests.post` nahi hai. Jab hum push karte hain, toh reliability ki zimmedari humari ho jati hai: customer ka server down ho sakta hai, slow ho sakta hai, galat status de sakta hai, ya koi attacker fake webhook bhej sakta hai. Isliye real webhook system mein chahiye: durable queue, retries with backoff, signatures, replay protection, per-endpoint rate limits, SSRF protection, aur delivery logs. Mera Project 4 exactly yahi infrastructure hai -- Stripe-style webhook delivery.
why_needed: Systems ke beech real-time notification chahiye bina continuous polling ke; webhook push model deta hai.
real_world_analogy: Courier wala ghar ki bell bajata hai jab parcel aata hai -- aapko har 10 minute darwaza khol ke check nahi karna padta.
how_it_works: Customer `POST /endpoints` se URL + event types register karta hai. Hum `POST /events` pe event store karte hain, har subscribed endpoint ke liye ek delivery row banate hain, aur dispatcher us URL pe JSON body + `webhook-id`, `webhook-timestamp`, `webhook-signature` headers ke saath POST karta hai. 2xx = delivered, warna retry.
in_this_project: Is project mein customer ko jo request milti hai woh `API_DOCUMENTATION.md` mein documented hai: body `{"id","type","created_at","data"}` aur teen Standard Webhooks headers. Body `Dispatcher.deliver` mein banti hai aur `Dispatcher._send` POST karta hai. Demo consumer `webhooks/receiver/app.py` dikhata hai customer side pe kya karna chahiye.
code_example:
# real, trimmed: webhooks/dispatcher/dispatcher.py (Dispatcher.deliver)
body = json.dumps({"id": c.event_id, "type": c.event_type,
                   "created_at": c.event_created_at.isoformat(),
                   "data": c.payload}, separators=(",", ":")).encode()
result = await self._send(c, body)
advantages: Customer ko polling infra nahi banana padta
Server pe bekaar requests nahi aati
disadvantages: Sender ko reliability own karni padti hai
Customer ko public HTTPS endpoint expose karna padta hai
Security (signing, SSRF) ka extra kaam
common_mistakes: Webhook ko fire-and-forget samajhna, bina retry ke
Signature na bhejna, jisse koi bhi fake event bhej sake
follow_up_questions: How is a webhook different from a message queue subscription?
What happens if the customer's server is down?
How does the receiver know the webhook really came from you?

question: Polling vs webhooks: when would you use each?
answer_hinglish:
Polling mein customer har N second humse puchhta hai "kuch naya hua?"; webhook mein hum event hote hi customer ko push karte hain. Default choice webhook hai jab events kam aur unpredictable hon aur latency matter kare; polling tab theek hai jab client ke paas public endpoint nahi hai ya woh apni speed pe batch mein data chahta hai.

Polling ki problem: agar customer har 10 second poll karta hai aur din mein 5 events hote hain, toh 8640 requests mein se 8635 ka jawab "kuch nahi" hai -- waste. Aur latency average 5 second tak. Webhook mein ek event = ek request, aur latency milliseconds.

Lekin webhook free nahi hai. Jab hum push karte hain, toh customer ka server down ho toh retry humein karna hai, slow ho toh timeout humein lagana hai, aur ordering/duplicates ka contract humein define karna hai. Polling mein reliability client ki thi -- woh fail hua toh agli baar phir puchh lega.

Practical production answer: dono saath. Webhook notification ke liye, aur ek list/fetch API reconciliation ke liye -- agar koi webhook miss ho gaya ya out-of-order aaya, customer latest state fetch kar le. Stripe bhi yahi karta hai.
why_needed: Latency aur wasted requests ke beech trade-off samajhna har integration design ka pehla decision hai.
real_world_analogy: Polling = har 5 minute mein post office jaake puchhna 'mera letter aaya?'. Webhook = postman khud ghar pe deliver kar deta hai, lekin ghar pe koi nahi hai toh postman ko dobara aana padega.
how_it_works: Polling: client loop chalata hai, `GET /changes?since=...`. Webhook: server event pe outbound POST karta hai, failures pe retry schedule follow karta hai, aur client 2xx se acknowledge karta hai.
in_this_project: `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` ka pehla section 'Polling vs webhooks' yahi reasoning likhta hai: webhook se 'WE own reliability (retries, signing, ordering, endpoint failures). This system is that ownership.' Reconciliation ke liye project `GET /events/{id}` aur `GET /deliveries` deta hai, aur README ki known limitation kehti hai consumers `created_at` / fetch latest state use karein.
advantages: Polling: simple, client control mein, firewall-friendly
disadvantages: Webhook: sender pe reliability ka bojh
Polling: wasted requests aur latency
common_mistakes: Sirf webhook pe depend karna bina reconciliation API ke
Polling interval itna chhota rakhna ki server pe load ho jaye
follow_up_questions: How would a customer recover webhooks missed during their outage?
What is long polling and where does it fit?
Why do providers still offer list APIs alongside webhooks?

question: What is HMAC and why do webhook providers sign their requests?
answer_hinglish:
HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) ek keyed hash hai: `HMAC_SHA256(secret, message)`. Sirf woh log jinke paas secret hai same output bana sakte hain. Webhook mein yeh prove karta hai ki request sach mein humne bheji hai aur raste mein body change nahi hui.

Problem kya hai? Customer ka webhook URL public internet pe hai. Koi bhi us URL pe `{"type":"order.paid"}` POST kar sakta hai. Agar customer bina check kiye order ship kar de, toh attacker free maal le jayega. Isliye har endpoint ka ek shared secret hota hai (registration pe milta hai), hum har request ka HMAC bhejte hain, aur customer same secret se HMAC calculate karke compare karta hai.

Plain SHA256 kaafi kyun nahi? Kyunki hash bina secret ke koi bhi calculate kar sakta hai -- attacker body badle aur naya hash laga de. HMAC mein secret mixed hai, toh bina secret ke valid tag nahi ban sakta. Aur HMAC length-extension attacks se bhi safe hai jo naive `sha256(secret + body)` mein hote hain.

Is project mein secret 32 random bytes hai (256-bit), aur signing Standard Webhooks format follow karti hai -- id aur timestamp bhi signed hote hain, sirf body nahi.
why_needed: Public URL pe aane wali request authentic hai ya forged, yeh receiver ko pata hona chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Purane zamane ki wax seal: letter pe raja ki muhar. Muhar sirf raja ke paas hai, toh seal sahi hai matlab letter asli aur khola nahi gaya.
how_it_works: Sender: `tag = HMAC_SHA256(key, signed_content)`, header mein bhejo. Receiver: same key se tag recompute karo, constant-time compare karo. Match nahi hua toh 401.
in_this_project: `services/signing.py::sign` yeh karta hai: `hmac.new(_key(secret), signed, hashlib.sha256).digest()` aur base64. `generate_secret` `secrets.token_bytes(32)` use karta hai. Receiver side `verify` aur demo `receiver/app.py` 401 return karta hai agar signature match nahi hota; `test_roundtrip_and_tamper_detection` body/id/secret change karke rejection prove karta hai.
disadvantages: Shared secret dono side pe store karna padta hai
Non-repudiation nahi (dono ke paas same key)
common_mistakes: sha256(secret + body) jaise naive construction use karna
Signature `==` se compare karna (timing leak)
Parsed JSON ko re-serialize karke verify karna
follow_up_questions: Why not use asymmetric signatures (Ed25519) instead?
What does the timestamp in the signed content protect against?
How do you rotate a leaked secret without downtime?

question: Explain at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery. Which one does this system give?
answer_hinglish:
Teen semantics hain. At-most-once: ek baar bhejo, fail hua toh bhool jao -- message kho sakta hai, duplicate kabhi nahi. At-least-once: tab tak retry karo jab tak acknowledgement na mile -- message kabhi nahi khoyega, lekin duplicate aa sakta hai. Exactly-once: har message ek hi baar effect kare -- network ke across yeh "delivery" level pe possible nahi, sirf "effect" level pe dedupe se achieve hota hai.

Mera system at-least-once deta hai. Kyun? Event aur delivery rows ek transaction mein commit hote hain, toh kuch khota nahi. Dispatcher crash ho jaye toh lease expire hone pe doosra dispatcher re-claim karta hai. Customer ka 2xx raste mein kho jaye toh hum retry karenge -- aur customer ko woh event dobara milega.

Toh duplicates ka solution? Har request mein `webhook-id` header hota hai jo event id hai aur retries/replays mein same rehta hai. Customer us id pe dedupe kare -- "agar yeh id pehle process ho chuki hai toh 200 return karo aur kuch mat karo". Isse customer side pe effectively-once effect milta hai.

Interview line: "Delivery at-least-once, processing effectively-once via idempotent receiver.
why_needed: Har distributed messaging design ka contract yahi teen options mein se ek hota hai; galat samjha toh duplicates ya data loss.
real_world_analogy: Registered post: postman tab tak aata rahega jab tak aap sign na karo (at-least-once). Agar aapne sign kiya lekin receipt postman se kho gayi, woh dobara aayega -- aap ko 'yeh toh mil gaya' bolna hai (dedupe).
how_it_works: At-least-once = durable state + retry until ack. Ack lost => redelivery. Dedupe key receiver ko duplicate pehchanne deta hai.
in_this_project: `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` Guarantees table: 'Delivery: at-least-once (lease + retries); duplicates possible -> webhook-id for dedupe'. `receiver/app.py` `app.state.seen` mein ids rakhta hai aur duplicate pe `200 duplicate ignored` deta hai. `test_receiver_dedupes_replayed_delivery` delivered delivery ko dobara pending karke prove karta hai ki receiver ne `duplicates == 1` count kiya.
advantages: Dedupe key se receiver effectively-once bana sakta hai
disadvantages: Receiver ko idempotent banana padta hai
Dedupe store ka retention sochna padta hai
common_mistakes: 'Exactly-once delivery' claim karna
Receiver ka dedupe sirf memory mein rakhna production mein
follow_up_questions: Why is exactly-once delivery to a third party impossible?
How long should the receiver keep seen webhook ids?
Where can duplicates come from in your system?

question: What is SSRF and why is it the main security risk for a webhook sender?
answer_hinglish:
SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) tab hota hai jab attacker humare server ko kisi aisi jagah request bhejwa deta hai jahan attacker khud nahi pahunch sakta -- jaise internal network ya cloud metadata service.

Webhook system SSRF ka perfect target hai, kyunki uska poora kaam hi hai "customer ke diye hue URL pe request bhejna". Socho customer endpoint register karta hai `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/`. Yeh AWS ka metadata service hai jo sirf andar se accessible hai. Humara dispatcher wahan POST karega aur response snippet delivery log mein store karega -- attacker dashboard pe jaake humare IAM credentials padh lega. Ya `http://localhost:6379/` dekar humare Redis pe commands bhejwa de.

Defence layers is project mein: sirf https (http sirf dev mein), URL mein credentials nahi, aur sabse important -- send time pe DNS resolve karke check ki IP public hai; loopback, private, link-local, IPv4-mapped IPv6 sab block. Redirects follow nahi karte, kyunki public URL 302 se internal pe bhej sakta hai. Production mein network layer pe bhi egress block karna chahiye -- defence in depth.
why_needed: Customer-controlled URL + humare server ki network position = attacker ko andar ka access, agar guard na ho.
real_world_analogy: Aap office ke receptionist ho aur koi phone pe bolta hai 'CEO ke cabin ka safe khol ke andar ki file mujhe padh ke sunao'. Receptionist ke paas andar access hai, caller ke paas nahi -- isliye receptionist ko rule chahiye ki kahan jaana allowed hai.
how_it_works: Attacker URL control karta hai -> server request bhejta hai -> internal service (metadata, Redis, admin panel) trust karti hai kyunki request andar se aayi -> response ya side effect attacker tak.
in_this_project: `services/ssrf.py` ka docstring exactly yeh example deta hai (169.254.169.254, localhost:6379). `validate_url_syntax` registration pe, aur `assert_public_destination` har send se pehle `Dispatcher._send` mein chalta hai. `httpx.AsyncClient(follow_redirects=False)`. Test `test_ssrf_blocks_internal_destinations` 9 internal URLs block karta hai.
advantages: Guard ek central jagah pe (send path)
Cloud credentials leak jaisa critical risk band
disadvantages: DNS resolve har send pe -- thoda latency
Legit internal customers (on-prem) support nahi
common_mistakes: Sirf registration pe URL check karna
Redirects follow karna
Response body pura store/return karna
follow_up_questions: What is DNS rebinding?
Why block IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses?
What network-level controls would you add?

question: Where do you need idempotency in a webhook system? Name both boundaries.
answer_hinglish:
Do boundaries hain jahan retries hote hain, aur dono pe idempotency chahiye.

Pehla: publisher -> humara API. Humari internal service `POST /events` call karti hai, timeout aa gaya, woh retry karti hai. Agar hum dono baar naya event bana dein toh customer ko do "order.paid" webhooks jayenge alag ids ke saath -- customer dedupe bhi nahi kar payega. Isliye `idempotency_key`: same key dobara aaye toh original event return karo (200 instead of 201), naye delivery rows nahi.

Doosra: humara dispatcher -> customer ka endpoint. Hum at-least-once deliver karte hain, toh customer ko duplicates milenge. Iske liye stable `webhook-id` header -- event id, jo retries aur manual replays mein same rehta hai. Customer us id pe dedupe karta hai.

Dhyan do: dono alag problems solve karte hain. Idempotency key upstream duplicates (do events) rokta hai; webhook-id downstream duplicates (ek event ki do deliveries) ko pehchanne deta hai. Agar sirf webhook-id ho aur publish idempotent na ho, toh duplicate event ka webhook-id alag hoga aur receiver ka dedupe kaam nahi karega. Yeh distinction interview mein strong signal hai.
why_needed: Har retry boundary pe duplicate ka risk hai; ek boundary miss ki toh end-to-end duplicates aate hain.
real_world_analogy: Bank cheque number: aap galti se do baar same cheque jama karo (publish retry) toh bank number dekh ke dusri baar reject karta hai. Aur bank ka SMS do baar aaye (delivery retry) toh transaction id same hai, aap samajh jaate ho ek hi transaction hai.
how_it_works: Publish: unique `idempotency_key` column + pehle lookup + `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. Delivery: `webhook-id = event_id`, receiver ek seen-set rakhta hai.
in_this_project: `services/events.py::publish` key check karta hai aur `(event, n, False)` return karta hai; route `create_event` tab status 200 set karta hai. `test_publish_idempotency_key` dono calls ke baad sirf 1 delivery row assert karta hai. `Dispatcher._send` mein `msg_id = c.event_id` header banta hai, aur `receiver/app.py` usi pe dedupe karta hai.
advantages: Publisher bina dar ke retry kar sakta hai
disadvantages: Publisher ko stable key generate karni padti hai
Same key + different payload ko project detect nahi karta (original return hota hai)
common_mistakes: Idempotency key random per-retry generate karna (bekaar)
Sirf ek boundary pe idempotency sochna
follow_up_questions: How do you handle two concurrent requests with the same idempotency key?
Should the same key with a different payload be an error?
How long should idempotency keys be kept?

question: How should a webhook sender interpret HTTP status codes from the receiver?
answer_hinglish:
Rule simple hai: 2xx = delivered, baaki sab = failure aur retry -- kuch special cases ke saath.

Is project mein: 200-299 -> `success`, delivery `succeeded`. Koi bhi doosra status (4xx, 5xx) -> `http_error`, retry schedule ke hisaab se agla attempt. Timeout aur connection error bhi failure hain aur retry hote hain.

Special cases: `410 Gone` ka matlab customer explicitly bol raha hai "yeh endpoint ab exist nahi karta, mat bhejo" -- hum delivery dead karte hain aur poora endpoint disable kar dete hain. `429 Too Many Requests` aur `503 Service Unavailable` ke saath agar `Retry-After` header hai, toh agla attempt kam se kam utni der baad -- customer ne back-off maanga hai, respect karna chahiye.

Kyun 4xx ko bhi retry karte hain? Kyunki webhook receivers aksar galti se 400/401/404 dete hain -- deployment ke beech route missing, ya secret update nahi hua. Retry se unhe fix karne ka time milta hai. Yeh trade-off hai: permanent 4xx pe kuch attempts waste hote hain, lekin data loss nahi. Redirects (3xx) follow nahi hote -- SSRF ki wajah se -- toh 3xx bhi failure hai.
why_needed: Status code hi sender ka ek matra signal hai ki agla step kya ho; galat interpretation = data loss ya customer pe flood.
real_world_analogy: Courier ko jawab: 'le liya' (2xx), 'abhi busy hoon, 2 ghante baad aana' (429 + Retry-After), 'yeh banda yahan rehta hi nahi' (410 -- address hi cancel), 'darwaza band hai' (5xx -- baad mein phir try).
how_it_works: `_send` status code se `SendResult` banata hai; `_record` decide karta hai success/retry/dead; `_next_delay` Retry-After apply karta hai; `RECORD_SQL` 410 pe endpoint disable karta hai.
in_this_project: `Dispatcher._send`: `if 200 <= resp.status_code < 300: return SendResult("success", ...)`, warna `http_error` with `retry_after_s=_retry_after(resp)`. `_record` mein `gone = r.status_code == 410` aur gone pe delay None (dead). Tests: `test_410_gone_disables_endpoint`, `test_429_retry_after_is_honoured`, `test_transient_failures_then_success`.
advantages: 410 se customer khud unsubscribe kar sakta hai
disadvantages: Permanent 4xx pe bhi attempts waste
3xx ko failure maanna kuch customers ko surprise karta hai
common_mistakes: Redirect follow karna
Retry-After ignore karna
Sirf 5xx retry karna aur 4xx pe drop kar dena
follow_up_questions: Why not stop retrying on 400?
What if Retry-After is an HTTP date?
How does 410 differ from auto-disable?

question: What is the dual-write problem?
answer_hinglish:
Dual-write problem tab hota hai jab ek business action ko do alag systems mein likhna padta hai -- jaise database aur message queue -- aur dono writes ek atomic transaction mein nahi ho sakte. Beech mein crash hua toh dono inconsistent ho jaate hain.

Webhook example: API pehle Postgres mein event insert karti hai, commit karti hai, phir Redis/Kafka mein "deliver this" message daalti hai. Agar commit ke baad aur publish se pehle process crash ho gaya -- event DB mein hai lekin queue mein nahi, webhook kabhi nahi jayega. Ulta order karo (pehle queue, phir DB) toh crash pe queue mein message hai jiska event DB mein nahi -- ghost webhook chala jayega jiska record hi nahi.

Retry karke fix kyun nahi? Kyunki process crash ho gaya, retry karne wala bacha hi nahi. Aur 2-phase commit (XA) zyada tar queues support nahi karte aur slow/fragile hai.

Solution: ek hi system mein likho. Transactional outbox: event aur "kaam" (delivery rows) dono same Postgres transaction mein. Phir alag process outbox padhke deliver karta hai. Mere project mein outbox hi queue hai, isliye relay process bhi nahi chahiye.
why_needed: Jab bhi DB + broker dono mein likhna ho, yeh silent data loss ka sabse common source hai.
real_world_analogy: Aap bank mein paise jama karte ho aur cashier passbook update karke receipt dena bhool jaye (ya receipt de de aur passbook update na ho). Dono kaam ek saath hone chahiye, ek register mein.
how_it_works: Write A commit -> crash -> write B kabhi nahi. Do independent systems ke beech atomicity nahi hoti jab tak distributed transaction na ho.
in_this_project: `services/events.py` ka module docstring yahi kehta hai: 'No saved the event but lost the queue message'. `publish` event aur saari `Delivery` rows ek hi `AsyncSession` transaction mein insert karta hai (route dependency `session` `s.begin()` khol ke rakhti hai). `LEARNING_GUIDE.md` Step 2 isi problem ko explain karta hai.
code_example:
# illustrative: the BROKEN dual write this project avoids
async def publish_broken(db, broker, body):
    await db.insert_event(body)
    await db.commit()
    # crash here -> event exists, nobody ever delivers it
    await broker.send("deliveries", body)
advantages: Pehchanne se silent data loss rokte ho
Outbox pattern ki motivation clear hoti hai
disadvantages: Solution (outbox) se DB pe load badhta hai
Relay chahiye agar queue alag system ho
common_mistakes: Sochna ki 'try/except mein retry' se fix ho jayega
Commit ke baad broker publish ko 'almost atomic' maanna
follow_up_questions: How does the transactional outbox solve it?
What about Change Data Capture (Debezium)?
Why not two-phase commit?

question: How does the transactional outbox pattern work in this project?
answer_hinglish:
Outbox pattern: business data aur "bhejna hai" wala record same database transaction mein likho; phir ek alag process us outbox ko padh ke bahar bhejta hai. Commit hua toh dono hain, rollback hua toh dono nahi -- dual write khatam.

Mere project mein ek twist hai: `deliveries` table hi outbox hai aur wahi work queue bhi. `publish()` ek transaction mein: (1) `events` mein row insert, (2) subscribed endpoints dhundho (array overlap), (3) har endpoint ke liye `deliveries` mein `pending` row. Route ki `session` dependency `s.begin()` ke andar chalti hai, toh API 201 return kare uske pehle commit ho chuka hota hai.

Phir dispatchers seedha `deliveries` table ko `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` se claim karte hain. Classic outbox mein ek "relay" hota hai jo outbox rows Kafka mein daalta hai -- woh ek aur at-least-once hop hai. Yahan relay nahi, kyunki Postgres khud queue hai.

Proof: `test_publish_is_atomic` publish ke baad commit se pehle RuntimeError raise karta hai, aur phir assert karta hai ki events aur deliveries dono tables mein 0 rows. Trade-off: har delivery DB load hai; bahut high scale pe outbox se Kafka mein relay karna padega.
why_needed: Event accept karne ke baad 'promise' hai ki deliver hoga -- outbox woh promise atomic banata hai.
real_world_analogy: Restaurant ka order slip: waiter order book mein likhta hai aur wahi slip kitchen ki queue hai. Alag se kitchen ko phone nahi karna padta jo bhool sakte ho.
how_it_works: BEGIN; INSERT event; INSERT N delivery rows; COMMIT. Consumer: SELECT due rows FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, process, mark done. Crash before commit = nothing promised.
in_this_project: `services/events.py::publish` + `db/models.py::Delivery` (docstring: 'This table IS the outbox and the work queue'). Test `tests/test_publish_api.py::test_publish_is_atomic`. `TRADEOFFS.md` #1 aur `ARCHITECTURE.md` decision 1 isko explain karte hain.
code_example:
# real, trimmed: webhooks/services/events.py::publish
stmt = (insert(Event).values(id=event_id, type=body.type, payload=body.payload,
                             idempotency_key=body.idempotency_key)
        .on_conflict_do_nothing(index_elements=["idempotency_key"]).returning(Event.id))
...
subscribed = select(Endpoint.id).where(Endpoint.event_types.overlap([body.type, "*"]))
endpoint_ids = (await s.scalars(subscribed)).all()
if endpoint_ids:
    await s.execute(insert(Delivery), [{"event_id": event_id, "endpoint_id": eid} for eid in endpoint_ids])
advantages: Atomic publish, koi lost delivery nahi
Audit aur SQL queries free (sab ek DB mein)
disadvantages: Har delivery = DB writes; vacuum churn
Fan-out bada ho (10k endpoints) toh ek transaction bhaari
common_mistakes: Outbox likhna lekin relay ko at-most-once banana
Outbox rows kabhi prune na karna

What happens if one event fans out to 50,000 endpoints?
How is this different from CDC?

question: How does FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED let several dispatchers share one Postgres table as a queue?
answer_hinglish:
`FOR UPDATE` selected rows pe row-level lock le leta hai transaction ke end tak. Normal case mein doosra transaction un rows pe `FOR UPDATE` kare toh woh wait karta hai. `SKIP LOCKED` kehta hai: "jo rows locked hain unhe chhod do, aage ki free rows de do". Isse N dispatchers ek hi query chalate hain aur har ek ko disjoint batch milta hai -- bina kisi coordinator ke.

Mere `CLAIM_SQL` mein inner SELECT due rows (pending + due, ya in_flight + lease expired) `ORDER BY next_attempt_at LIMIT :batch FOR UPDATE OF d2 SKIP LOCKED` se uthata hai, aur outer UPDATE unhe `in_flight` mark kar deta hai, `attempts + 1` aur `locked_until = now() + lease` set karta hai. Transaction turant commit hota hai.

Important baat: row lock sirf claim transaction tak hai (milliseconds). Uske baad protection `status='in_flight'` + `locked_until` lease deti hai -- doosra dispatcher in_flight row ko tab tak nahi uthata jab tak lease expire na ho.

Bina SKIP LOCKED: dispatchers ya toh ek doosre pe block karte (serialize), ya plain SELECT + UPDATE mein race se same row do baar claim hoti. `test_three_dispatchers_deliver_each_exactly_once` 3 dispatchers x 150 events chalata hai aur har webhook-id exactly ek baar dekhta hai.
why_needed: Multiple workers bina double processing aur bina blocking ke kaam baant sakein -- yahi queue ka core.
real_world_analogy: Bank mein token counters: har clerk agla free token uthata hai; jo token kisi aur clerk ke haath mein hai use skip karke agla le leta hai, wait nahi karta.
how_it_works: Inner SELECT row locks leta hai; locked rows skip; outer UPDATE claimed rows ko state change karta hai; COMMIT pe lock release lekin status/lease ab doosron ko rok raha hai.
in_this_project: `dispatcher/dispatcher.py::CLAIM_SQL`, `Dispatcher.claim` (`async with self.sm() as s, s.begin()` -- ek short transaction). `FOR UPDATE OF d2` sirf deliveries ko lock karta hai, joined `endpoints` row ko nahi -- warna ek endpoint ki saari deliveries same endpoint row pe contend karti.
code_example:
-- real, trimmed: CLAIM_SQL inner select
SELECT d2.id FROM deliveries d2
  JOIN endpoints e ON e.id = d2.endpoint_id AND e.enabled
 WHERE (d2.status = 'pending' AND d2.next_attempt_at <= now())
    OR (d2.status = 'in_flight' AND d2.locked_until < now())
 ORDER BY d2.next_attempt_at
 LIMIT :batch
 FOR UPDATE OF d2 SKIP LOCKED
advantages: Strict ordering ki zaroorat nahi toh perfect
disadvantages: Har claim ek write transaction
Global FIFO strict nahi (skipped rows)
High churn pe vacuum load
common_mistakes: FOR UPDATE bina SKIP LOCKED -- dispatchers serialize
Lock poore HTTP call tak pakad ke rakhna
FOR UPDATE ko join ki saari tables pe lagana (OF clause bhoolna)
follow_up_questions: Why is OF d2 important?
Why commit immediately instead of holding the lock during the send?
What does SKIP LOCKED do to ordering?

question: What is a lease (locked_until) and why do you need it once the row lock is released?
answer_hinglish:
Lease ek time-bound ownership hai: "yeh delivery dispatcher X ki hai `locked_until` tak". Claim transaction commit hote hi row lock chala jata hai, toh kuch aur chahiye jo doosre dispatchers ko roke aur crash ke baad recover kare -- woh lease hai.

Flow: `CLAIM_SQL` row ko `status='in_flight'`, `locked_by=worker`, `locked_until=now()+30s` set karta hai. Jab tak lease valid hai, claim query ki condition `(in_flight AND locked_until < now())` false hai, toh koi aur nahi uthata. Delivery khatam hone pe `RECORD_SQL` `locked_until=NULL` kar deta hai.

Agar dispatcher HTTP call ke beech crash ho gaya? Row `in_flight` reh jaati hai. 30 second baad lease expire, aur kisi bhi dispatcher ki agli claim query use phir utha leti hai -- `attempts + 1` ke saath. Koi heartbeat service ya coordinator nahi chahiye; time hi recovery mechanism hai.

Lease length kaise chuni? Request timeout 10s hai (connect 3s), lease 30s -- comfortably zyada, taaki normal slow delivery ke beech lease expire na ho. Agar lease timeout se chhota hota toh healthy dispatcher ke chalte hue doosra dispatcher duplicate bhej deta. Lease expiry ke baad bhi zombie result likhne ki koshish kare toh fencing token (attempts) rokta hai.
why_needed: Crash recovery bina coordinator ke, aur short DB transactions -- dono lease se milte hain.
real_world_analogy: Library book issue: 14 din ki due date. Aap gayab ho gaye toh due date ke baad library book ko 'available' maan ke kisi aur ko de deti hai.
how_it_works: Claim: set owner + expiry. Done: clear owner. Crash: expiry pass -> claim query fir match karti hai -> re-claim with attempts+1.
in_this_project: `config.py` mein `lease_seconds: float = 30.0` (comment: 'expired -> another dispatcher retries'), `request_timeout_seconds = 10.0`. `CLAIM_SQL` `locked_until = now() + make_interval(secs => :lease)`. Test `test_crashed_dispatcher_lease_expires_and_zombie_result_is_rejected` lease 0.2s rakhta hai, A claim karke 'crash' karta hai, 0.3s baad B deliver karta hai with `attempts == 2`.
code_example:
# real, trimmed: tests/test_dispatcher.py
a = dispatcher(sm, limiter, receiver([secret]), wid="A", lease_seconds=0.2)
[claimed] = await a.claim()                 # A claims ... and "crashes"
assert await a.claim() == []
await asyncio.sleep(0.3)                    # lease expires
b = dispatcher(sm, limiter, receiver([secret]), wid="B", lease_seconds=30)
assert await b.run_once() == 1
advantages: Lock HTTP call ke dauraan hold nahi hota
disadvantages: Lease expiry tak recovery delay (30s)
Lease < actual work time = duplicates
common_mistakes: Lease ko request timeout se chhota rakhna
Lease ke bina sirf status flag pe rely karna (crash pe row hamesha in_flight)
follow_up_questions: What happens if the lease expires while the original dispatcher is still sending?
Should the dispatcher extend (heartbeat) the lease?
How is the lease time compared -- whose clock?

question: Explain how the attempts column acts as a fencing token.
answer_hinglish:
Fencing token ek monotonically badhne wala number hai jo har naye owner ko milta hai; result tabhi accept hota hai jab writer ke paas abhi bhi latest token ho. Isse "zombie" -- woh process jiski lease expire ho gayi lekin usko pata nahi -- purana result likh ke naye result ko overwrite nahi kar sakta.

Is project mein `attempts` hi token hai. Claim pe `attempts = attempts + 1` hota hai aur dispatcher returned value (`c.attempt`) yaad rakhta hai. Record karte waqt `RECORD_SQL` ki condition hai `WHERE id = :id AND attempts = :attempt AND status = 'in_flight'`.

Scenario: Dispatcher A ne attempt 1 claim kiya, GC pause ya network hang mein 40s atak gaya. Lease (30s) expire, B ne re-claim kiya -> attempts = 2, deliver kiya, succeeded record kiya. Ab A jaagta hai aur `500 failed` likhna chahta hai attempt 1 ke saath. `attempts = 1` match nahi karta (2 hai) aur status `succeeded` hai -- 0 rows updated. `_record` ise `stale` count karta hai aur warning log karta hai. Saath mein attempt log INSERT aur endpoint health update bhi `FROM d` / `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM d)` pe depend karte hain, toh zombie ka kuch bhi nahi likhta.

Note: fencing customer ko duplicate HTTP request jaane se nahi rokta -- woh sirf humare DB state ko protect karta hai. Customer ke liye dedupe `webhook-id` se.
why_needed: Leases akele safe nahi hain: process pause (GC, network) ke baad zombie writes state corrupt kar sakte hain.
real_world_analogy: Hotel ka room key card: naya guest check-in karta hai toh naya card banta hai aur purana card automatically invalid. Purana guest wapas aaye toh darwaza nahi khulta.
how_it_works: Token claim pe increment; write `WHERE token = my_token` (compare-and-set); mismatch = stale, discard.
in_this_project: `dispatcher.py` module docstring point 3, `CLAIM_SQL` mein `attempts = d.attempts + 1` aur `RETURNING ... d.attempts`, `RECORD_SQL` ki WHERE clause, `Dispatcher._record` mein `if not updated: self.stats["stale"] += 1; log.warning("stale_delivery_result")`. Test: `a._record(claimed, SendResult("http_error", 500, error="late")) == "stale"` aur delivery `succeeded` hi rehti hai.
code_example:
-- real, trimmed: RECORD_SQL first CTE
WITH d AS (
  UPDATE deliveries
     SET status = :status, ..., locked_until = NULL, locked_by = NULL
   WHERE id = :id AND attempts = :attempt AND status = 'in_flight'
  RETURNING id),
a AS (INSERT INTO delivery_attempts (...) SELECT id, :attempt, ... FROM d)
SELECT count(*) FROM d
advantages: Extra column nahi chahiye -- attempts already tha
disadvantages: Customer ko duplicate request phir bhi ja sakti hai
Manual replay `attempts=0` reset karta hai -- token monotonic nahi rehta (dekho observation)
common_mistakes: Sirf `locked_by = me` check karna (same worker id restart ke baad match ho sakta hai)
Fencing ko exactly-once ka guarantee samajhna
follow_up_questions: Does fencing prevent the duplicate HTTP request?
What happens to the token when an operator replays a delivery?
Where else have you used fencing tokens (Project 3)?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Alag `lease_token` column ki jagah `attempts` reuse karna schema simple rakhta hai, lekin do concepts (retry count aur ownership) ek column mein mix ho jaate hain. Rate limit refund `attempts - 1` karta hai, toh token decrement bhi hota hai -- yeh tabhi safe hai kyunki refund `WHERE attempts = c.attempt` se fenced hai aur row turant pending ho jati hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Observation: `retry_delivery` aur `replay_dead` `attempts=0` set karte hain. Agar koi bahut purana zombie attempt 1 hold kar raha ho aur replay ke baad naya claim phir attempt 1 de, toh theoretically zombie ka write match ho sakta hai. Practically zombie ko lease (30s) se kaafi zyada atakna padega, lekin strict fencing ke liye alag monotonic `claim_seq` column better hai.
advanced.alternatives: Alag UUID lease token (claim pe naya UUID, record pe match), ya Postgres advisory locks, ya DB-generated sequence. Redis-based queues (Project 3) mein token Lua script mein increment hota hai.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Scale se fencing ka cost nahi badhta -- ek WHERE predicate hai. 100x pe stale rate metric (`stale` stat) monitor karna zaroori, kyunki badhta stale rate batata hai ki lease bahut chhota hai ya dispatchers overloaded hain.
advanced.production_improvements: Monotonic `claim_seq` jo replay pe bhi kabhi reset na ho; `stale_delivery_result` pe alert; lease ko p99 send time ke basis pe tune karna.

question: Why is exactly-once delivery to a third-party HTTP endpoint impossible?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki sender kabhi pakka nahi jaan sakta ki receiver ne process kiya ya nahi, jab acknowledgement raste mein kho jaye. Yeh Two Generals problem ka practical form hai.

Scenario: hum POST bhejte hain. Customer ka server request receive karta hai, database mein order "paid" mark karta hai, aur 200 bhejta hai. Lekin 200 humare tak pahunchne se pehle connection reset ho jata hai, ya humara 10s timeout fire ho jata hai. Humare paas do options: retry karo (customer ko duplicate milega) ya mat karo (agar customer ne actually process nahi kiya tha toh event kho gaya). Humare side se dono cases bilkul same dikhte hain -- timeout. Koi bhi protocol yeh ambiguity khatam nahi kar sakta jab tak receiver humare saath ek atomic transaction mein na ho, jo third party ke saath possible nahi.

Isliye industry "at-least-once delivery + idempotent receiver" choose karti hai. Hum retry karte hain (kuch nahi khota), aur stable `webhook-id` dete hain taaki customer duplicate pehchaan sake. Exactly-once *effect* customer side pe tab milta hai jab woh webhook-id ko apne business write ke same transaction mein store kare.

`TRADEOFFS.md` #2 literally kehta hai: "a 2xx can be lost after the customer processed it".
why_needed: Interviewers check karte hain ki candidate 'exactly-once' marketing claims ke peeche ki reality samajhta hai.
real_world_analogy: Aap kisi ko phone pe paise bhejne bolte ho aur call cut ho jati hai -- pata nahi bheja ya nahi. Dobara bolo toh shayad do baar chala jaye; na bolo toh shayad gaya hi nahi. Solution: transaction ID se check karo.
how_it_works: Sender ke observation space mein 'processed + ack lost' aur 'not processed' indistinguishable hain. Isliye retry zaroori, aur duplicates unavoidable; dedupe receiver pe.
in_this_project: `TRADEOFFS.md` #2, `FAILURE_SCENARIOS.md` #9 ('Customer got the request but our response was lost -> redelivered with same webhook-id; receiver dedupes'). Timeout case `_send` mein `httpx.TimeoutException` -> `timeout` outcome -> retry. `test_receiver_dedupes_replayed_delivery` dedupe path prove karta hai.
code_example:
# illustrative: receiver making the EFFECT exactly-once
async with db.begin():
    inserted = await db.execute(
        "INSERT INTO processed_webhooks(id) VALUES (:id) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING id",
        {"id": headers["webhook-id"]})
    if inserted.first() is None:
        return Response(status_code=200)      # duplicate: already applied
    await apply_business_effect(db, payload)  # same transaction as the dedupe row
disadvantages: Receivers ko dedupe implement karna padta hai
Duplicates ki frequency timeouts pe depend karti hai
common_mistakes: Receiver ka dedupe check aur business write alag transactions mein karna
Kafka ke 'exactly-once' ko third-party HTTP pe apply samajhna
follow_up_questions: How should the receiver store processed ids so the effect is exactly-once?
Why does a timeout create the ambiguity but a 500 does not?
What is the Two Generals problem?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: At-least-once + dedupe vs at-most-once: webhooks mein data loss usually duplicate se zyada mehenga hai (payment missed vs processed twice detected), isliye at-least-once.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Timeouts sabse bada duplicate source hain: customer slow tha (11s), humne 10s pe cut kiya, retry kiya -- customer ne dono process kiye agar dedupe nahi. Dispatcher crash after send but before record bhi duplicate deta hai (lease expiry re-send).
advanced.alternatives: Receiver-side transactional dedupe table; ya sender-provided idempotent APIs jahan receiver 'upsert by event id' karta hai; thin events + fetch-latest-state jisme duplicates harmless hain.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Scale pe duplicates absolute count mein badhte hain (1M deliveries x 0.1% timeout = 1000 duplicates/day). Receivers ko dedupe store ka TTL (e.g. retry window ~11h se zyada) plan karna padta hai.
advanced.production_improvements: Docs mein dedupe recipe dena, duplicate rate metric (attempts > 1 jahan pehla attempt timeout tha) track karna, aur timeout ko customer p99 latency ke hisaab se tune karna.

question: Describe the Standard Webhooks signature format you implemented.
answer_hinglish:
Standard Webhooks ek open spec hai (Svix aur kuch providers ne banaya) taaki har provider apna alag signing scheme na banaye. Main ise isliye follow karta hoon kyunki customers ke paas ready-made verify libraries hoti hain aur reference test vectors se main prove kar sakta hoon ki implementation sahi hai.

Teen headers: `webhook-id` (event id, retries mein stable), `webhook-timestamp` (is attempt ka unix seconds), `webhook-signature` (`v1,<base64>` -- space separated, ek se zyada ho sakte hain).

Signed content: `"{id}.{timestamp}.{raw_body}"`. Key: secret `whsec_` prefix hata ke base64-decode karke raw bytes. Signature: `base64(HMAC_SHA256(key, signed_content))`, aur aage `v1,` version prefix.

Kuch details jo interview mein value add karti hain: `v1` prefix scheme versioning ke liye hai -- kal asymmetric `v1a` aa jaye toh same header mein dono bhej sakte ho. Multiple signatures space-separated isliye ki secret rotation ke dauraan purane aur naye dono secrets se sign kar sakein. `whsec_` prefix secret ko identifiable banata hai (secret scanners leak pakad sakte hain) aur galti se base64 string ko raw key maan lene se bachata hai.

`test_standard_webhooks_reference_vector` spec ka official vector use karta hai -- `v1,g0hM9SsE+OTPJTGt/tmIKtSyZlE3uFJELVlNIOLJ1OE=` exactly match hota hai.
why_needed: Interoperable, testable signing scheme -- custom crypto banane se bachata hai.
real_world_analogy: Jaise passport ka international format: har desh ka apna design ho sakta hai, lekin fields aur MRZ line standard hain taaki har airport machine padh sake.
how_it_works: signed = id + '.' + ts + '.' + body bytes; key = b64decode(secret[6:]); sig = 'v1,' + b64(hmac_sha256(key, signed)); header = ' '.join(sigs).
in_this_project: `services/signing.py` ka module docstring poora format likhta hai. `PREFIX = "whsec_"`, `_key` prefix strip karke decode karta hai, `sign`, `signature_header` (list of secrets ko join), `verify`. Reference vector test `tests/test_signing_ssrf.py::test_standard_webhooks_reference_vector`.
code_example:
# real: tests/test_signing_ssrf.py
def test_standard_webhooks_reference_vector():
    sig = sign("whsec_MfKQ9r8GKYqrTwjUPD8ILPZIo2LaLaSw", "msg_p5jXN8AQM9LWM0D4loKWxJek", 1614265330,
               b'{"test": 2432232314}')
    assert sig == "v1,g0hM9SsE+OTPJTGt/tmIKtSyZlE3uFJELVlNIOLJ1OE="
advantages: Customers existing libraries use kar sakte hain
disadvantages: Symmetric HMAC -- receiver bhi sign kar sakta hai
Header thoda bada during rotation
common_mistakes: Body ke bajaye parsed JSON sign karna
Secret ko base64 decode kiye bina string bytes as key use karna
Version prefix ignore karna
follow_up_questions: Why is the version prefix useful?
What would change if you used Ed25519 instead?
Why sign the id as well?

question: How does the timestamp in the signature give replay protection?
answer_hinglish:
Replay attack: attacker ek valid signed request capture kar leta hai (logs, proxy, compromised network) aur baad mein dobara bhejta hai. Agar sirf body signed hoti, toh woh request hamesha valid rahegi -- attacker "order.paid" ko 100 baar replay kar sakta hai.

Fix: timestamp ko signed content ke andar daalo (`id.timestamp.body`) aur receiver pe rule: agar `|now - timestamp| > tolerance` toh reject. Attacker timestamp badal nahi sakta kyunki woh MAC ke andar hai -- badla toh signature match nahi karega. Toh captured request sirf tolerance window (5 minute) ke andar replay ho sakti hai.

Bacha hua 5 minute ka window? Wahan `webhook-id` dedupe kaam aata hai -- same id dobara aaye toh receiver ignore karta hai. Dono milke full replay protection dete hain.

Do details: (1) check dono direction mein hai -- future timestamps bhi reject (`abs`), taaki attacker ko pre-signed future requests ka fayda na ho. (2) Timestamp har attempt pe naya hota hai (`int(time.time())` in `_send`), isliye 6 ghante baad ka retry bhi fresh timestamp ke saath valid hai. Tolerance 5 minute kyun? Clock skew aur network delay ke liye room, lekin replay window chhota.
why_needed: Signature akela authenticity deta hai, freshness nahi; replay rokne ke liye time binding chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Movie ticket pe show time likha hai -- kal ka ticket aaj valid nahi, chahe asli ho. Aur ticket number se gatekeeper dekh leta hai ki yeh ticket already scan ho chuka.
how_it_works: Receiver: parse ts -> `abs(now - ts) > 300` reject -> phir HMAC check. Sender: har attempt pe naya ts, naya signature.
in_this_project: `signing.py::verify`: `if abs(now - timestamp) > tolerance: raise VerificationError("timestamp outside tolerance (possible replay)")`, `DEFAULT_TOLERANCE_SECONDS = 300`. `test_replay_outside_tolerance_rejected` 301s past aur 301s future dono reject aur 300s accept prove karta hai. `_send` mein `ts = int(time.time())` per attempt.
code_example:
# real, trimmed: signing.verify
now = int(time.time()) if now is None else now
if abs(now - timestamp) > tolerance:
    raise VerificationError("timestamp outside tolerance (possible replay)")
advantages: Captured requests ka useful life sirf 5 minute
Stateless check -- receiver ko store nahi chahiye
disadvantages: Receiver ki clock galat ho toh legit requests reject
Window ke andar replay ke liye dedupe phir bhi chahiye
common_mistakes: Timestamp ko header mein bhejna lekin sign na karna
Sirf past check karna, future nahi
Retry pe purana timestamp reuse karna
follow_up_questions: What if the receiver's clock is 10 minutes off?
How do you close the 5-minute window completely?
Why is the timestamp per attempt and not per event?

question: Why must the receiver verify the signature over the raw request body?
answer_hinglish:
Kyunki signature exact bytes pe bana hai, JSON ke meaning pe nahi. Agar receiver pehle JSON parse kare aur phir `json.dumps(parsed)` karke verify kare, toh bytes badal sakte hain -- key order, whitespace, unicode escaping, number formatting (`1.0` vs `1`) -- aur valid signature bhi fail ho jayega.

Example: hum bhejte hain `{"id":"evt_1","type":"order.paid"}` (compact, `separators=(",", ":")`). Receiver ka framework parse karke dict bana deta hai; developer `json.dumps(dict)` karta hai jo default `", "` aur `": "` separators use karta hai -- ab body `{"id": "evt_1", "type": "order.paid"}` hai, HMAC alag, 401. Ya ulta danger: kuch frameworks body ko normalize karke deti hain aur developer sochta hai "kuch toh match ho gaya".

Security angle bhi hai: parse-then-verify mein parser ke quirks (duplicate keys, jaise `{"amount":1,"amount":1000}`) ka fayda uthaya ja sakta hai. Raw bytes verify karo, phir unhi bytes ko parse karo -- jo verify hua wahi use hoga.

Mere demo receiver mein `raw = await request.body()` pehle, `verify(..., raw)`, aur sirf successful verify ke baad `json.loads(raw)`. Yeh `receiver/app.py` docstring ka point 1 hai.
why_needed: Sabse common customer-side bug jo 'signature mismatch' tickets banata hai.
real_world_analogy: Notary ne document ke har page pe stamp kiya. Aap document retype karke (same content, different font) notary stamp claim nahi kar sakte -- original kagaz hi verify hota hai.
how_it_works: HMAC byte-sequence pe deterministic hai. Re-serialization byte sequence badalta hai. Isliye verify(raw) -> parse(raw).
in_this_project: `receiver/app.py::webhook`: `raw = await request.body()`, `verify(app.state.secrets, dict(request.headers), raw)`, phir `json.loads(raw)`. Sender side `Dispatcher.deliver` body ek baar bytes mein encode karta hai aur wahi bytes sign aur send hote hain. `SECURITY.md`: 'Re-serialisation breaking signatures -> verify the RAW body before parsing JSON'. `test_roundtrip_and_tamper_detection` ek extra space (`BODY + b" "`) se bhi failure dikhata hai.
advantages: Parser quirks ka attack surface band
disadvantages: Kuch frameworks (Express json middleware) raw body by default discard karte hain -- extra config
common_mistakes: Express mein `express.json()` ke baad `JSON.stringify(req.body)` verify karna
Proxy/middleware jo body re-encode karta hai (gzip, charset)
follow_up_questions: How do you get the raw body in Express or Django?
Why does the sender use compact separators?
Could the sender sign a canonical JSON form instead?

question: Why does the retry schedule add jitter, and what does the schedule look like?
answer_hinglish:
Jitter isliye ki retries synchronize na hon. Socho customer ka server 2 minute down tha aur us beech 10,000 deliveries fail huin. Bina jitter sab exactly 30 second baad retry karengi -- customer ka server jaise hi wapas aata hai, 10,000 requests ek second mein -- woh phir gir jata hai. Isse thundering herd kehte hain. +-20% random jitter un retries ko 24-36 second ke window mein spread kar deta hai.

Schedule: `retry_schedule_seconds = [5, 30, 120, 600, 1800, 3600, 3*3600, 6*3600]` -- yaani 5s, 30s, 2m, 10m, 30m, 1h, 3h, 6h. Pehla attempt + 8 retries = 9 attempts, roughly 11 ghante tak. Uske baad `dead`.

`_next_delay(attempt, result)`: agar `attempt > len(schedule)` toh None (dead), warna `schedule[attempt-1] * random.uniform(0.8, 1.2)`. Agar 429/503 ke saath Retry-After aaya toh `max(delay, retry_after)`.

Fixed schedule kyun, pure exponential kyun nahi? Predictability. Customer ko bata sakte ho "hum ~11 ghante tak retry karte hain" -- unka on-call jaanta hai kitna time hai fix karne ka. Schedule early mein aggressive hai (transient blips jaldi recover) aur baad mein spaced (lambi outage pe load nahi). `test_retry_schedule_with_backoff` 60s schedule pe gap 48-73s window assert karta hai.
why_needed: Retries correct timing ke bina khud outage ka cause ban sakti hain.
real_world_analogy: Stadium se match ke baad sab ek saath gate pe jaayein toh stampede. Announcement 'Block A pehle, Block B 5 minute baad' crowd spread kar deta hai.
how_it_works: delay_n = schedule[n-1] * U(0.8, 1.2); Retry-After ho toh max(delay, retry_after); n > len(schedule) -> dead. `next_attempt_at = now + delay`, claim query sirf due rows uthati hai.
in_this_project: `config.py::retry_schedule_seconds` (comment: 'Length+1 = max attempts'), `Dispatcher._next_delay`, `_record` mein `next_at = now + timedelta(seconds=delay)`. `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` Retry policy section. Tests: `test_retry_schedule_with_backoff`, `test_wrong_secret_is_rejected_by_receiver_and_retried` (3-step schedule -> 4 attempts -> dead).
disadvantages: Fixed schedule recovery speed adaptive nahi
Jitter se exact timing test karna mushkil (window assert)
common_mistakes: Jitter ke bina fixed delay
Unbounded retries (kabhi dead nahi)
Retry ke delay ko in-memory sleep se implement karna (crash pe lost)
follow_up_questions: Full jitter vs +-20% jitter -- difference?
Why store next_attempt_at in the DB instead of sleeping?
How long should the total retry window be?

question: Why doesn't this system guarantee webhook ordering? What is head-of-line blocking?
answer_hinglish:
Seedha jawab: ordering guarantee dene ke liye ek endpoint ki deliveries ko serialize karna padta -- event 2 tab tak nahi jayega jab tak event 1 succeed na ho. Agar event 1 fail ho raha hai (customer ka bug, ek specific payload pe 500), toh event 2, 3, ... 10,000 sab ruk jaate hain. Isse head-of-line (HOL) blocking kehte hain: queue ke aage ka ek stuck item poori line rok deta hai.

Is project mein ordering kahan tootti hai? (1) Retries: event 1 fail hua, 5s baad retry; event 2 turant succeed -- customer ko pehle 2 milta hai. (2) Multiple dispatchers parallel claim karte hain -- do events same millisecond mein alag dispatchers se ja sakte hain. (3) Ek dispatcher ke andar bhi batch `asyncio.gather` se concurrent bhejta hai.

Industry choice: unordered + har payload mein `created_at` + "fetch latest state". Customer ko `subscription.updated` mila toh woh payload pe blindly rely na kare, balki API se latest subscription fetch kare, ya `created_at` compare karke purana event ignore kare. Stripe bhi ordering guarantee nahi deta.

Agar customer ordering demand kare toh per-endpoint (ya per-entity key) FIFO bana sakte ho -- lekin throughput us endpoint ka 1 in-flight request tak gir jata hai aur ek poison event sab block karta hai. `TRADEOFFS.md` #3 yahi trade-off likhta hai.
why_needed: Ordering ek common customer ask hai; uski cost samjhana senior signal hai.
real_world_analogy: Toll booth ki ek hi lane: aage wali gaadi ka FASTag fail hua toh peeche 50 gaadiyan atak gayi. Multiple lanes (parallel) mein flow hai lekin pehle aayi gaadi pehle nikle, guarantee nahi.
how_it_works: Ordering = per-key serialization = max 1 in-flight per key + stuck head blocks all. Parallelism + retries = reordering.
in_this_project: `TRADEOFFS.md` #3, `SYSTEM_DESIGN.md` Guarantees ('Ordering: none across events (retries reorder)'), README known limitations. Body mein `created_at` `Dispatcher.deliver` se jata hai. `CLAIM_SQL` `ORDER BY next_attempt_at` sirf best-effort fairness hai, ordering guarantee nahi.
advantages: Ek stuck event baaki ko block nahi karta
disadvantages: Customers ko out-of-order handle karna padta hai
State-carrying events (updated) ke liye confusing
common_mistakes: Sochna ki ORDER BY created_at se ordering mil gayi
Customer ko payload state pe blindly trust karne dena
follow_up_questions: How would you implement per-entity ordering if a big customer demanded it?
What is a sequence number approach on the receiver?
How does Kafka partitioning give ordering and at what cost?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Ordered (per-endpoint FIFO) vs unordered: ordered mein throughput per endpoint = 1/latency (100ms latency -> 10/s max), aur poison event pe poori line 11 ghante tak ruk sakti hai. Unordered mein full concurrency.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Ordered mode mein agar head event `dead` ho jaye toh kya? Skip karo (ordering tooti) ya rok do (permanent block). Dono bure -- isliye operators ko manual intervention chahiye.
advanced.alternatives: Per-entity ordering (ordering key = order_id) -- sirf same entity ke events serialize; ya sequence numbers payload mein dekar receiver ko reorder/ignore karne do; ya thin events (sirf id) + fetch.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 100x pe per-key serialization ka matlab hai lakhon logical queues -- Kafka partitions by key se natural hai, lekin Postgres SKIP LOCKED design mein 'is key ka koi in-flight hai kya' check har claim pe expensive.
advanced.production_improvements: Payload mein monotonic `sequence` per entity add karna, docs mein 'events can arrive out of order' clearly, aur thin-event option.

question: Why is the webhook-id the event id and why must it stay the same across retries?
answer_hinglish:
`webhook-id` customer ke liye dedupe key hai. Agar woh har retry pe badalta, toh customer ke liye attempt 1 aur attempt 2 do alag webhooks dikhte, aur woh dono process kar deta -- duplicate charge, duplicate email.

Isliye is project mein `msg_id = c.event_id` -- event ka id, jo publish ke time ek baar `"evt_" + secrets.token_hex(12)` se banta hai aur kabhi nahi badalta. Retries, lease-expiry re-sends, aur operator ke manual replays sab mein same id jata hai. Customer ek simple rule follow kare: "is id ko pehle dekha hai toh 200 return karo, kuch mat karo".

Timestamp alag hai -- woh per attempt badalta hai (freshness ke liye). Isliye id stable aur timestamp fresh: dono ka role alag.

Ek subtle point: same event do endpoints ko jaye toh dono ko same webhook-id milta hai. Yeh theek hai kyunki dedupe har receiver apne andar karta hai. Aur id signed content mein hai, toh attacker id badal ke dedupe bypass nahi kar sakta -- `test_roundtrip_and_tamper_detection` id badal ke verification fail dikhata hai.
why_needed: At-least-once delivery ke saath dedupe tabhi possible hai jab duplicates ka identity same ho.
real_world_analogy: Courier ka AWB number: parcel teen baar delivery attempt ho, number wahi rehta hai, aap track kar lete ho ki ek hi parcel hai.
how_it_works: id publish pe generate -> deliveries table mein event_id -> claim returns event_id -> header webhook-id. Receiver: seen set lookup.
in_this_project: `events.py::publish` (`event_id = "evt_" + secrets.token_hex(12)`), `Dispatcher._send` (`msg_id = c.event_id`, header `webhook-id`), `signing.py` docstring ('stable per EVENT (same across retries) -> receivers dedupe on it'). `retry_delivery` route docstring: replay safe kyunki receivers webhook-id pe dedupe karte hain.
code_example:
# real, trimmed: Dispatcher._send
msg_id = c.event_id
ts = int(time.time())
headers = {"content-type": "application/json", "webhook-id": msg_id, "webhook-timestamp": str(ts),
           "webhook-signature": signature_header(self._active_secrets(c), msg_id, ts, body)}
disadvantages: Receiver ko seen ids store karne padte hain
common_mistakes: Har attempt pe naya uuid header
Delivery id (per endpoint row) ko webhook-id banana jo replay pe... (yahan bhi stable hota, lekin event-level id zyada meaningful)
follow_up_questions: Why not use the delivery row id as webhook-id?
How long should receivers remember ids?
What if the publisher creates two events for the same business fact?

question: What is a dead letter state and how does replay work here?
answer_hinglish:
Dead letter = woh delivery jiske saare attempts khatam ho gaye ya jo permanently undeliverable hai. Usse hamesha retry karte rehna capacity waste hai, aur chup chaap delete karna data loss. Isliye ek alag terminal state `dead` -- visible, queryable, aur replayable.

Is project mein delivery `dead` hoti hai jab: (1) retry schedule khatam (`_next_delay` None return kare), (2) endpoint ne `410 Gone` diya, (3) SSRF guard ne destination `blocked` kiya. Dead row `deliveries` table mein hi rehti hai (alag DLQ table nahi) -- `status='dead'`, last error aur status code ke saath, aur poora attempt history `delivery_attempts` mein.

Replay do tarike: `POST /deliveries/{id}/retry` ek delivery ko (dead ya succeeded) `pending`, `attempts=0`, `next_attempt_at=now()` kar deta hai; agar delivery abhi pending/in_flight hai toh 409 Conflict. `POST /endpoints/{id}/replay-dead` ek endpoint ki saari dead deliveries ek UPDATE mein requeue karta hai -- typical use: customer ki 6 ghante ki outage khatam, unhone fix deploy kiya, ab sab bhej do. Dashboard mein dead rows pe "Replay" button hai.

Replay safe kyun? Same `webhook-id` jata hai, receiver dedupe karta hai.
why_needed: Permanent failures ko visible aur recoverable rakhna -- na infinite retry, na silent drop.
real_world_analogy: Post office ka 'undelivered' section: letter wahan rakha hai, aap address theek karke dobara bhejne bol sakte ho.
how_it_works: Terminal status in same table; replay = status reset with UPDATE ... WHERE status IN ('dead','succeeded'); rowcount 0 => 409.
in_this_project: `routes.py::retry_delivery` (409 via `Conflict` agar rowcount 0), `routes.py::replay_dead`, `Dispatcher._record` dead logic, dashboard `retry(id)` JS function. Tests: `test_api_flow` (pending pe retry -> 409), `test_receiver_dedupes_replayed_delivery`.
code_example:
# real: webhooks/api/routes.py
res = await s.execute(update(Delivery).where(Delivery.id == delivery_id, Delivery.status.in_(["dead", "succeeded"]))
                      .values(status="pending", attempts=0, next_attempt_at=func.now(), last_error=None))
if res.rowcount == 0:
    raise Conflict("delivery not found or still pending/in flight")
disadvantages: Dead rows table mein jama hote hain -- retention chahiye
replay-dead disabled endpoint ko enable nahi karta -- dono steps chahiye
common_mistakes: Dead letters ko monitor na karna
Replay ke time attempts reset karna aur fencing implications bhoolna
follow_up_questions: What happens if you replay-dead while the endpoint is still disabled?
Should replay reset attempts to 0?
How would you replay only a time range?

question: Why does each endpoint get its own token bucket, and why is it in Redis?
answer_hinglish:
Per-endpoint rate limit isliye ki humara dispatcher customer ka DDoS na ban jaye. Socho customer 3 ghante down tha, 50,000 deliveries pending hain. Woh wapas aata hai aur hamare dispatchers poori speed (100+/s) se uspe toot padte hain -- uska chhota server phir gir jata hai. Har endpoint ka `rate_limit_per_second` (default 10/s, customer set kar sakta hai 1000 tak) us flood ko smooth karta hai.

Token bucket kyun: bucket mein `cap` tokens, `rate` per second refill, har request ek token. Burst allow karta hai (cap tak) aur long-run rate limit karta hai. Yahan `burst = max(1, per_second)` -- yaani 10/s endpoint ko ek second ka burst.

Redis kyun, memory kyun nahi? Kyunki multiple dispatchers hain. Agar har dispatcher apna local bucket rakhe toh 3 dispatchers x 10/s = 30/s customer pe. Budget per endpoint *shared* hona chahiye -- Redis ek central atomic counter hai. Lua script poora read-refill-consume-write atomic karta hai, taaki do dispatchers ek hi token na le lein. Yeh wahi idea hai jo Project 1 (rate limiter) mein tha.

Agar token nahi mila? Delivery fail nahi hoti -- attempt refund karke `wait_ms` baad pending kar dete hain. Throttling humari policy hai, customer ki galti nahi.
why_needed: Backlog flush mein customer ko protect karna aur multiple dispatchers mein ek hi budget enforce karna.
real_world_analogy: Ek building mein ek hi lift hai aur 3 security guards log bhej rahe hain. Har guard apna count rakhe toh lift overload; ek shared register (Redis) mein entry hogi tabhi limit sahi.
how_it_works: Lua: Redis TIME se now, HMGET tokens/ts, lazy refill `elapsed * rate / 1000` (cap tak), token ho toh -1 aur wait=0, warna wait = ceil((1 - tokens) * 1000 / rate) ms. HSET + PEXPIRE.
in_this_project: `services/ratelimit.py` (`_LUA`, `EndpointRateLimiter.acquire`, key `wh:rl:{endpoint_id}`), `Dispatcher.deliver` pehla step `self.limiter.acquire(...)`. `test_per_endpoint_rate_limit_does_not_burn_attempts`: 2/s endpoint, 10 events -> sirf 2 sent, 8 pending with `attempts == 0`.
code_example:
-- real: token bucket Lua in webhooks/services/ratelimit.py
local t = redis.call('TIME'); local now = t[1] * 1000 + math.floor(t[2] / 1000)
local s = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(s[1]) or cap; local ts = tonumber(s[2]) or now
tokens = math.min(cap, tokens + math.max(now - ts, 0) * rate / 1000)
local wait = 0
if tokens >= 1 then tokens = tokens - 1 else wait = math.ceil((1 - tokens) * 1000 / rate) end
disadvantages: Har delivery pe ek Redis round trip
Redis dependency (fail-open se mitigate)
common_mistakes: Local in-memory limiter with multiple dispatchers
Rate limited delivery ko failed attempt count karna
follow_up_questions: Why fail open when Redis is down?
Why use Redis TIME instead of the client clock?
What happens to throughput when many deliveries hit an empty bucket?
